meta.title: Who really said "I had four gold medals, but you can't eat four gold medals"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Jesse Owens really said it — but not in 1936. ESPN and the IOC print the line; Wikiquote dates it to a 1971 interview no one has ever identified.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I had four gold medals, but you can't eat four gold medals'?
meta.ogDescription: Owens said it, but not on returning from Berlin. Traced to a 1971 interview that no source names — and no transcript or recording has ever surfaced.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1913–1980 · American sprinter · four golds at Berlin 1936
answer.sourceLine: Owens almost certainly said this, or something very close to it — ESPN’s SportsCentury, the IOC’s own Olympics.com, Wikipedia and Wikiquote all carry the line in his voice, and it fits a documented life. But it is a look back, not a remark from 1936: Wikiquote and Biography.com date it to a 1971 interview, and neither names the interviewer, the outlet or a transcript. The article they lean on prints the words with no date at all, so no primary source pins this exact wording.

source.heading: The paper trail

docMeta.dd: An interview, dated 1971 by Wikiquote and Biography.com; interviewer and outlet unnamed
None located — no transcript, recording or contemporaneous printing

source.excerpt: “People said it was degrading for an Olympic champion to run against a horse, but what was I supposed to do?” Owens said. “I had four gold medals, but you can’t eat four gold medals.”
trail: The standard printing is Larry Schwartz’s ESPN SportsCentury profile “Owens pierced a myth” ↗, which quotes him: “People said it was degrading for an Olympic champion to run against a horse, but what was I supposed to do?” … “I had four gold medals, but you can’t eat four gold medals.” Schwartz gives no date and names no interview.

Wikiquote ↗ lists the line with the citation “Interview (1971); also quoted in ‘Owens pierced a myth’ by Larry Schwartz in ESPN SportsCentury”, and does not flag it as disputed or misattributed. Biography.com ↗ likewise says “in an interview in 1971”. Neither names the interviewer or the publication.
The IOC’s Olympics.com ↗ introduces the same words with “So said Jesse Owens in later life” — framing it as a reflection, not a remark made in 1936.

The episode behind the line is squarely on the record. An Associated Press dispatch in the Rocky Mountain News of 27 December 1936 ↗ reports Owens beating a five-year-old gelding over 100 yards in Havana the previous day, off a 40-yard handicap, in 9.9 seconds — the horse named there as “Julio Macaw”.
source.excerptNote: That is ESPN’s wording. The IOC’s Olympics.com ↗ prints the passage as one continuous quotation beginning “People say it was degrading…”, and Wikipedia ↗ adds a further sentence, “There was no television, no big advertising, no endorsements then. Not for a black man, anyway.”, which it sources to Jon Entine’s Taboo (PublicAffairs, 2000), p. 187.
source.rightsNote: Not public domain, and not confidently classifiable either. The wording comes from an interview Owens gave in later life — dated 1971 by the sources that carry it, far past the 1931 US public-domain line — but that interview has never been identified, so there is no work, publication date or rights holder to name. The printings that actually circulate, including ESPN’s SportsCentury profile ↗, are themselves in copyright. Quote the sentence with attribution; do not treat it as rights-free.

author.name: Jesse Owens
author.heading: Jesse Owens
author.metaLine: 1913–1980 · American sprinter · four Olympic golds, Berlin 1936
author.bio: Born James Cleveland Owens in Oakville, Alabama in 1913, Owens won the 100 metres, 200 metres, long jump and 4×100 metre relay at the 1936 Berlin Olympics — four golds in eight days, in front of Adolf Hitler. What followed was not a fortune. His amateur status was stripped within weeks of the Games, endorsements never came, and he spent the late 1930s racing local sprinters, motorbikes and, in Havana, a racehorse for cash, before working as a petrol-station attendant, a playground janitor and a dry-cleaning manager. Only in the 1950s did public speaking and a Chicago public-relations business bring security; he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1976 and died in Tucson, Arizona in 1980.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is claiming this line — the credit to Jesse Owens is not in serious doubt. What travels wrongly is when he said it, how much of it he said, and how thin the sourcing underneath it really is.

items.why: It is regularly shared as Owens’s reaction on stepping off the boat from Berlin. It is a look back from decades afterwards: the IOC’s Olympics.com ↗ prefaces the same words with “So said Jesse Owens in later life”, and both Wikiquote and Biography.com ↗ place it in a 1971 interview.

“I had four gold medals, but you can’t eat four gold medals” is the back half of an answer about the Havana horse race. ESPN ↗ prints it directly after “People said it was degrading for an Olympic champion to run against a horse, but what was I supposed to do?”, and Wikipedia ↗ carries a third sentence — “There was no television, no big advertising, no endorsements then. Not for a black man, anyway.” — which it sources to Jon Entine’s Taboo (PublicAffairs, 2000), p. 187.

AZQuotes ↗ shows the bare sentence and credits nothing but the ESPN web article — no interview, no date, no transcript. The aggregators are recycling a secondary retelling, and Quote Investigator ↗ has never taken the line up, so there is no specialist finding to lean on either.

misattribution.truthLine: Owens said it — the credit is solid, and the hardship behind it is documented down to the 9.9 seconds he ran against a horse in Havana. What is missing is a primary record: the ESPN SportsCentury profile that the quote sites cite, “Owens pierced a myth” ↗, carries the words with no date and no named interview, and nothing better has surfaced since.

context.heading: Why the line stings
lead: Berlin, August 1936: Owens won the 100 metres, the 200 metres, the long jump and a relay gold and came home the most famous athlete alive. It bought him almost nothing. His amateur status was withdrawn after he declined a post-Games European tour, the commercial offers that had tempted him home dried up within months, and he took work as a petrol-station attendant, a playground janitor and the manager of a dry-cleaning firm.

On 26 December 1936, at the opening of Cuba’s international sports week in Havana, he lined up beside a five-year-old gelding, took a forty-yard start and won the hundred yards in 9.9 seconds. Reflecting on those years later in life he said: “Sure it bothered me. But at least it was an honest living. I had to eat.” The gold-medals line is that same answer, sharpened to a point — which is exactly why it travels, and exactly why it gets stripped of its date.
context.detailsSummary: Why this is filed as attributed rather than verified
detailsBody: The credit to Owens is not seriously in doubt. What is missing is the record. Wikiquote annotates the line “Interview (1971)” and points to Larry Schwartz’s ESPN SportsCentury profile; Schwartz’s article prints the words with no date, no interviewer and no publication. Biography.com repeats “in an interview in 1971” and adds nothing further. No transcript, recording, newspaper report or book citation for that interview has surfaced.

Two slightly different renderings also circulate. ESPN has “People said it was degrading…”; Olympics.com and Wikipedia have “People say it was degrading…”. Wikipedia carries a further sentence — “There was no television, no big advertising, no endorsements then. Not for a black man, anyway.” — which it sources to Jon Entine’s Taboo (PublicAffairs, 2000), p. 187. Small drift of that kind is the signature of a quotation passed hand to hand rather than read off a page.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists "I had four gold medals, but you can't eat four gold medals" with the citation "Interview (1971); also quoted in 'Owens pierced a myth' by Larry Schwartz in ESPN SportsCentury", and does not flag it as disputed or misattributed.

Larry Schwartz's ESPN SportsCentury profile quotes Owens: "People said it was degrading for an Olympic champion to run against a horse, but what was I supposed to do?" Owens said. "I had four gold medals, but you can't eat four gold medals." — with no date, interviewer or occasion given. The same piece records Owens saying he wasn't invited to shake hands with Hitler but wasn't invited to the White House either, and gives his birth (12 Sept 1913, Oakville, Ala.) and death (31 March 1980, Tucson, Ariz.).

Olympics.com prints "People say it was degrading for an Olympic champion to run against a horse, but what was I supposed to do? I had four gold medals, but you can't eat four gold medals." and introduces it with "So said Jesse Owens in later life". It also states his amateur status was swiftly withdrawn after he declined to compete in Sweden, lists his later jobs (petrol station attendant, playground janitor, dry cleaning manager), and quotes "Sure it bothered me... But at least it was an honest living. I had to eat."

Biography.com states that "In an interview in 1971" Owens said "I had four gold medals, but you can't eat four gold medals. There was no television, no big advertising, no endorsements then. Not for a Black man, anyway." — without naming the interviewer, programme or publication.

An Associated Press dispatch headlined "Jesse Owens Outspeeds Race Horse in Havana Exhibition" in The Rocky Mountain News (Daily), 27 December 1936, page 17, reports that on 26 December Owens beat a five-year-old gelding in a 100-yard dash at the opening of Cuba's international sports week, was given a 40-yard handicap and covered the course in 9.9 seconds; the horse is named "Julio Macaw".

English Wikipedia carries the blockquote "People say it was degrading for an Olympic champion to run against a horse, but what was I supposed to do? I had four gold medals, but you can't eat four gold medals." sourced to Olympics.com, and the follow-on sentence "There was no television, no big advertising, no endorsements then. Not for a black man, anyway." sourced to Jon Entine, Taboo (PublicAffairs, 2000), p. 187. It also gives his birth name James Cleveland Owens, birth 12 Sept 1913 in Oakville, Alabama, death 31 March 1980 in Tucson, Arizona, the four 1936 gold events, Avery Brundage having him permanently suspended from amateur competition, and the 1976 Presidential Medal of Freedom.

AZQuotes displays the bare one-line version "I had four gold medals, but you can't eat four gold medals." and cites only "Owens pierced a myth" by Larry Schwartz at www.espn.com — no interview, date, book or transcript.
A site search of Quote Investigator for "Jesse Owens" returns only articles about the "Find the Good" saying; QI has no article investigating "you can't eat four gold medals".
